replacements.before: Connectedness. $A$ is path-connected if any two points are joined by a continuous path inside $A$; path components are the maximal path-connected subsets (for open sets they coincide with the usual connected components, in general not). Continuous images of path-connected sets are path-connected, so a continuous parameterisation from $\mathbb R^N$ reaches only one path component of a set that has several. A finite grid has no paths; its connectivity depends on an adjacency rule, and certified reachability is a third notion (Module 6, Module 4, Module 13, Module 11).
replacements.after: Connectedness. $A$ is path-connected if any two points are joined by a continuous path inside $A$; path components are the maximal path-connected subsets (for open sets they coincide with the usual connected components, in general not). Continuous images of path-connected sets are path-connected, so a continuous parameterisation from $\mathbb R^N$ reaches only one path component of a set that has several. A finite grid in Euclidean space has no continuous path joining distinct points; its connectivity depends on an adjacency rule, and certified reachability is a third notion (Module 6, Module 4, Module 13, Module 11).
replacements.reason: Every grid point has a constant continuous path. A finite Euclidean grid is discrete, so any continuous path from the connected unit interval into it is constant and cannot join distinct points. Graph adjacency and certified reachability remain separate.
